title: KV snapshot reconcile and heterogeneous retry playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for fast, low-risk recovery from memory pressure / OOM events that leverages: incremental local KV snapshots, a reconcile pass after restart, and a heterogeneous retry ladder that prefers light-weight fallbacks (e.g., quantized kernel, shorter context, cached-prefix responses) before full-request retries or global circuit trips. The aim is to minimize tail latency impact for in-flight requests while keeping throughput predictable.

Context / motivation:
- We see a class of incidents where a single large request (long sequence + large KV) or a small storm of concurrent requests pushes a worker to OOM and the eviction/restart leads to large replay and cold-KV misses, creating cascading failures.
- Current approaches (simple restart + full-cache flush) cause a thundering herd of cache warmups and repeated kernel loads. That increases p99s and can cause global capacity churn.
- Need a pragmatic middle-ground: keep most requests available, reduce rework, and gracefully degrade quality where necessary.

Goals:
- Allow node-level restarts to recover quickly without global traffic disruption.
- Ensure in-flight requests have a predictable fallback ladder that preserves latency SLOs.
- Reconcile local KV state with cluster-level authoritative state within a bounded window.
- Avoid aggressive global circuit opens unless systemic.

Non-goals:
- This is not a full replacement for long-term cached-persistent stores (we still expect persistent warm caches for Dedicated).
- Not addressing application-level semantically-correct retry idempotency here — callers must still use idempotency keys when appropriate.

Assumptions:
- Workers maintain an in-memory KV cache with optional local snapshotting to ephemeral disk (fast NVMe).
- There is a control-plane component that tracks model variant compatibility and a simple node heartbeat stream.
- Kernel binary/quantized artifacts can be loaded from local cache or pulled remotely; load time is non-trivial (50-300ms).

High-level flow (failure + recovery):
1) Pre-failure (proactive): lightweight periodic local snapshots of KV hot prefixes written every N seconds (default 10s) to ephemeral NVMe. Snapshots are small: only top-k prefix entries, using LRU heuristics.
2) Failure detection: OOM or forced process restart triggers: worker marks node as soft-unavailable and emits failure event with short metadata (active requests count, last-snapshot-id, kernel-version).
3) In-flight handling: frontend/edge switches to worker fallback ladder described below rather than immediately retrying. Edge keeps requests pinned to original worker for a short grace window (100ms) to allow fast restarts.
4) Restart & reconcile: upon restart, worker attempts to load last local snapshot and begins a background reconcile with cluster-level KV digest. Reconcile is incremental and limited by a budget (ioops/time) so it never blocks serving.
5) Serving while reconciling: newly arriving requests are served using a graded fallback ladder. If reconcile provides a matching prefix during request lifetime, a fast patch is applied.
6) Escalation: if multiple nodes in the same routing group fail within a short window, the control plane moves from node-level fallbacks to opening a regional circuit breaker for the offending model SKU.

Fallback ladder (per-request): ordered from least-impact to most-impactful
- 0: Continue on same worker after restart if kernel and snapshot restored within grace window (best-case).
- 1: Use cached prefix-only response: if prefix tokens exist in local snapshot, compute continuation but with conservative decoding parameters (smaller beam, lower max-tokens).
- 2: Switch to quantized kernel variant of same model (faster memory footprint but slight quality loss). Kernel load is prioritized and served with lower concurrency.
- 3: Shorten context window: drop oldest context segments (prefers dropping non-system longest prefix) to fit memory budget — log context-trim decisions for QA.
- 4: Proxy request to sibling node (same variant) if capacity available. This is a hedged request with de-duplication at the edge to avoid double-costing when both finish.
- 5: Last resort: return structured retry instruction to caller (Retry-After or retry-token) and increment local circuit meter.

Retry semantics and backoff patterns:
- Prefer client-visible soft fallbacks over automatic aggressive exponential retries that can worsen pressure.
- When automatic retries are used, use heterogeneous backoff: first retry uses short fixed jitter (50-150ms) aimed to catch fast restarts; subsequent retries escalate to randomized exponential with upper cap (2s).
- Retries are capped by token-cost heuristics: do not retry requests estimated to cost more than threshold T (configurable) to avoid resource waste.

Checkpointing strategy details:
- Snapshot content: top-k prefixes + compacted KV entries referenced by active requests. Keys are versioned with snapshot-id.
- Frequency: adaptive — faster (5s) under high mem-pressure, slower (30s) during quiet times.
- Write durability: ephemeral NVMe only; these are hints to avoid full cold-warm cycles. Do not assume snapshots survive host reboot in Private mode unless configured to persistent store.
- Snapshot size target: aim for < 8MB per snapshot for common worker types; configure limits based on instance class.

Reconcile algorithm (background):
- Worker opens a delta-stream with the routing control-plane (digest-based).
- The control-plane responds with authoritative prefix digests for the model+version. Worker pulls relevant missing entries on demand with rate limits.
- Reconcile operates in rounds; each round has IO and CPU budget so it cannot starve serving threads.

Circuit & meter logic:
- Node-level meter aggregates: restart count, OOM occurrences, reconcile lag, snapshot-hit-rate, active-requests-trim-rate.
- Circuit thresholds are multi-dimensional: single restart alone does not trip a regional circuit; but combined high restart rate + high reconcile-lag + low snapshot-hit-rate in a 60s window triggers a regional circuit open.
- Circuit states: CLOSED -> SOFT_OPEN (route lowered to 50% traffic with forced fallbacks) -> OPEN (route diverted to other regions/variants). Auto-recovery with cooldown window plus manual review flag for enterprise tenants.

Kernel and scheduling interactions:
- Kernel loads are prioritized by request criticality. Low-latency interactive requests get earlier kernel pull tokens. Background reconcile/kernel prefetch uses leftover capacity.
- To avoid repeated kernel thrash after OOMs, we implement a tiny kernel warm-backoff: recently-failed kernel versions are penalized for a cooldown period before being pulled eagerly on restart.

Observability & metrics to add (critical):
- snapshot.write.latency, snapshot.size.bytes
- snapshot.hit_rate (local serving using snapshot)
- reconcile.rounds_per_minute, reconcile.io_bytes
- fallback.ladder.step.count (histogram of which fallback used)
- node.restart.count, node.oom.count, node.reconcile_lag_seconds
- regional.circuit.state and traffic_fraction_post_circuit
- request.retry_count_by_cost_bucket

Operational runbook (short):
- On node OOM alert: check snapshot hit_rate, last_snapshot_id, reconcile_lag.
- If last_snapshot_id present and restore success -> expect fast recovery; monitor fallback.ladder.step for increased usage.
- If reconcile_lag >> 30s and multiple nodes affected -> consider temporary regional circuit and scale up Dedicated capacity.
- For persistent kernel thrash: inspect kernel_warmbackoff logs and increase penalty window for offending kernel version.

Implementation notes / rough tasks:
- [ ] implement compact incremental snapshot writer (C++ runtime) + small API to expose last_snapshot_id to control plane.
- [ ] control-plane digest API for incremental reconcile (protobuf + streaming).
- [ ] fallback ladder config knobs exposed to routing layer (percentages, timeouts).
- [ ] edge de-duplication logic for hedged requests (idempotency token).
- [ ] end-to-end test harness simulating OOM storms with parametric sequences.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Snapshot durability vs speed: should we optionally persist to S3/NAS for Dedicated? Pros: faster rebuild across host restarts; cons: added complexity and staleness handling.
- How to account for cost when hedged requests finish both: billing vs visible latency. Need product guidance.
- How to tune fallback quality knobs (quantized kernel params, context trim heuristics) per-customer vs global defaults.

Next steps & milestones (short):
- Prototype local snapshot writer and a minimal reconcile server (2 weeks).
- Add fallback ladder enforcement in the edge routing (1 week after prototype).
- Chaos tests + perf runs to measure p50/p95/p99 impact (2 weeks).

Notes to self:
- Keep this playbook intentionally conservative: prefer user-visible degraded quality to repeat heavy-cost work.
- Collect many examples from recent incidents and attach to Confluence page.

References:
- Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUN/KV+Snapshot+Design
- Jira: INF-2317 (OOM reconciliation epic)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/398
